title: Annually resolved atmospheric CO2 growth rate over the past nine centuries
abstract: Interannual atmospheric <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>CO</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math> growth rate (CGR), mostly resulting from fluctuating carbon uptake in terrestrial biosphere, is a key determinant of atmospheric <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>CO</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math> concentration. However, CGR observations are merely available in recent decades, which are unable to fully reveal its natural variability and interactions with terrestrial ecosystems and climatic drivers. Here we present a reconstruction of interannual CGR over the past nine centuries (1100-2006) based on a globally distributed temperature-sensitive proxy network. The reconstruction is validated by the comparison with dynamic global vegetation model simulations and the El Niño-Southern Oscillation. Our data reveal a close association of CGR variability with atmospheric <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>CO</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math> concentration and tropical climate. Present CGR variability is unprecedentedly high over the past nine centuries, suggestive of the instability of present carbon cycle and the reducing resilience of atmospheric carbon balance under intensifying anthropogenic forcing. Our record provides a pre-industrial constraint for perceiving the climate-carbon coupling under historical climate forcings.
problem: The short duration of modern atmospheric CO₂ growth rate (CGR) observations hinders a full understanding of its long-term natural variability and its interactions with climate, making it difficult to contextualize the current state and distinguish anthropogenic effects from natural cycles.
method: This study proposes a reconstruction method using a global network of temperature-sensitive proxy records and principal components regression to create a continuous, annually resolved atmospheric CO2 growth rate record for the past nine centuries (1100-2006).
task: The task is to reconstruct the annually resolved atmospheric CO₂ growth rate over the past nine centuries (1100-2006) using a global temperature-sensitive proxy network to understand its natural variability, climatic drivers, and long-term context.
innovation: This study presents an annually resolved reconstruction of the atmospheric CO2 growth rate over the past nine centuries, revealing that its current variability is unprecedentedly high and providing a pre-industrial context for understanding long-term climate-carbon interactions.

Several tree-ring proxies in northern mid- to high-latitude regions are also selected, which are attributed to ENSO teleconnections7,26 or other large-scale climate variability15. Proxies available in Africa and South America are sparse and only a few are selected for CGR reconstruction. Since interannual climate and carbon variability in the two continents is strongly impacted by ENSO and tropical climate11,27, our CGR reconstruction captures carbon fluxes in these regions reasonably well owing to the incorporation of a wide range of proxy records that are sensitive to ENSO, CGR, and tropical climate at a global scale. Future expansion of proxy network in these regions will inevitably improve the accuracy of CGR reconstruction.

Results demonstrate that tropical precipitation is negatively correlated with CGR due to the water limitation on terrestrial carbon uptake, and tropical temperature exhibits positive correlations with CGR (Fig. 3a, b). The correlations with scPDSI indicate that positive CGR are associated with drought in the northeastern South America, western and southern Africa, Southeast Asia, and Australia, a pattern identifiable to the typical impacts of El Niño (Fig. 3c). Partitioning the scPDSI into four vegetated land cover classes in tropical and extra-tropical regions shows that tropical forests, mainly consisting of evergreen broadleaf forests, have the highest correlations with CGR (Fig. 3d; Supplementary Fig. 9). The scPDSI in other tropical vegetated regions exhibits significant but weaker correlations to CGR and may partly contribute to its variability. Therefore, tropical forests play a major role in modulating interannual CGR variations due to their high carbon productivity 7,8.

A decoupling was observed between CGR and climatic conditions in two years (1991 and 1992) impacted by the Mount Pinatubo eruption7,9 (Supplementary Fig. 1), which suggests that the PAGES 2k proxy records are unable to capture the full impacts of volcanic eruptions on solar radiation and CGR variations in despite of their sensitivity to temperature changes. Therefore, these two years impacted by the Mount Pinatubo eruption are excluded from regression model development.

Nonetheless, the effects of injecting aerosols on CGR are minimal after the eruptions of Mount Agung (1963) and El Chichón (1982), suggesting that only major eruptions at the magnitude of Mount Pinatubo could considerably enhance terrestrial carbon sink and disrupt the climate-driven CGR. Since Pinatubo-size eruptions have merely occurred 20 times or less over the past nine centuries35-37, our reconstruction is unlikely undermined by such rare perturbations as shown through a sensitivity test (Supplementary Fig. 3; Methods).
